claims.source: RGCs with larger RFs tended to display greater anticipation, with RF size accounting for 35% of the observed variance in the delays for motion (Pearson's r = −0.593, n = 25, Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The three cells that failed to show any motion anticipation also had the smallest RF size.
claims.source: The three cells that failed to show any motion anticipation also had the smallest RF size.
claims.evidence: Observation from experimental data.

claims.claim: The peak EPSC lags behind the receptive field centre by 79 ± 17 μm in OFF ganglion cells during motion.
claims.source: Example of the EPSC recorded as a bar moves across the receptive field of an OFF ganglion cell (average of six presentations). The peak EPSC lags behind the receptive field centre by 79 ± 17 μm (1.2 ± 0.3º, n = 7).
claims.evidence: Measured experimentally from voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: The motion evoked EPSC was not significantly different from the expected linear response in most RGCs, indicating that lateral inhibition is not present.
claims.source: The motion evoked EPSC was not significantly different from the expected linear response, indicating that lateral inhibition is not present (using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, n = 7).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of measured and predicted EPSCs.

claims.claim: Orientation selective cells showed a clear indication of lateral inhibition.
claims.source: Orientation selective cells did show a clear indication of lateral inhibition (n = 2).
claims.evidence: Observed in recordings from two orientation-selective cells shown in Figure 1I.

claims.claim: In 7 out of 9 RGCs the peak excitatory input was delayed, occurring 158 ± 34 ms after the bar reached the receptive field centre.
claims.source: In 7 out of 9 RGCs the peak excitatory input was delayed, occurring 158 ± 34 ms after the bar reached the receptive field centre (Figure 1H, black trace), demonstrating that the fast gain reduction in the EPSC was not sufficient to generate motion anticipation.
claims.evidence: Measured from voltage-clamp recordings.

claims.claim: Disrupting inhibition in a single ganglion cell by dialyzing with 120 mM Cl− greatly enhanced the response to a moving bar.
claims.source: We then disrupted inhibition in this single ganglion cell by going into whole-cell mode and dialyzing the cell with an intracellular solution containing 120 mM Cl− (Figure 2A, grey). The advantage of this approach over pharmacology or genetic manipulation is that it acutely disrupts the inhibition impinging on a single RGC while leaving excitatory inputs and the rest of the retinal circuitry intact; a similar approach was used to demonstrate direction selectivity occurs postsynaptically in direction-selective RGCs (Taylor et al., 2000). Disrupting inhibitory inputs greatly enhanced the response to a moving bar, indicating that under normal circumstances inactivation of Nav channel does not attenuate the RGC response to motion.
claims.evidence: Experimental manipulation shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: With inhibition disrupted, the location of the peak firing became delayed occurring 210 ± 26 ms after the stimulus had reached the RF centre.
claims.source: Importantly, with inhibition disrupted, the location of the peak firing became delayed occurring 210 ± 26 ms after the stimuli had reached the RF centre (Figure 2C, p < 0.0002).
claims.evidence: Measured experimentally after disrupting inhibition, shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The delay for a flash was unaffected by disrupting inhibition.
claims.source: In contrast, for the four cells tested, the delay for a flash was unaffected by disrupting inhibition (64.4 ± 8.7 ms vs 62.7 ± 5.2 ms, Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: Measured experimentally before and after disrupting inhibition.

claims.claim: Feedforward inhibition from amacrine cells to RGCs plays the major role in correcting for the lag in phototransduction.
claims.source: We conclude that feedforward inhibition from amacrine cells to RGCs plays the major role in correcting for the lag in phototransduction allowing the retina to correctly signal the position of a moving object.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing that disrupting inhibition eliminates motion anticipation.

claims.claim: The inhibitory-to-excitatory conductance ratio measured over the RF centre was 2.1 ± 0.23.
claims.source: The time-course of synaptic conductance changes used in simulations mimicked those measured experimentally (Figure 3A), and the average density of synaptic inputs over the dendritic trees also matched known distributions with around one excitatory synapse per 5 µm of dendrite (Freed and Sterling, 1988; Jakobs et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2008) and a ∼2:1 ratio of excitatory to inhibitory synapses, reflecting the ratio of the inhibitory to excitatory conductance measured over the receptive field centre (Figure 3B, 2.1 ± 0.23, n = 10).
claims.evidence: Measured experimentally from voltage-clamp recordings.

claims.claim: Passive properties of dendrites are sufficient to account for motion anticipation.
claims.source: When the receptive field of these model neurons was probed by mimicking flashed bars, it reproduced a Gaussian receptive field similar to that measured experimentally (Figures 1, 3D). Crucially, the EPSPs arriving at the soma displayed motion anticipation when tested with our standard moving bar stimulus (Figure 3D), demonstrating that the passive interactions of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs are sufficient to generate motion anticipation.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling with passive dendrites.

claims.claim: The ability of feedforward inhibition to generate motion anticipation was robust to variations in membrane resistance (Rm) and intracellular resistance (Ri), but was destroyed once Rm fell to 50 MΩ.
claims.source: The ability of feedforward inhibition to generate motion anticipation was robust to variations in both Rm and Ri over this range, but was destroyed once Rm fell to 50 MΩ (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: Tested through computational modeling with varying parameters.

claims.claim: Active dendritic conductances are not necessary for motion anticipation.
claims.source: To test directly whether active conductances were required to generate motion anticipation, we recorded from ganglion cells whose dendrites were made passive by dialysis of 2 mM MK-801 and 10 mM QX-314-Bromide; together these, substances block NMDA receptors and voltage-sensitive Na+ and Ca2+ channels (Talbot and Sayer, 1996; Kuzmiski et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Experimental manipulation blocking active conductances while motion anticipation persisted.

claims.claim: All cells with passive dendrites had EPSPs that peaked significantly earlier than the expected linear response.
claims.source: All cells had EPSPs that peaked significantly earlier than the expected linear response (p = 0.0002, n = 7), occurring 47 ± 29 ms before the stimuli reached the RF centre and this was not significantly different to the time of peak spike rate observed for the cells in Figure 1 (47 ± 29 ms, n = 7 vs 46 ± 13 ms, n = 25, p = 0.9844).
claims.evidence: Measured experimentally from cells with passive dendrites.

claims.claim: Motion anticipation operated when the bar moved at velocities between 3.8° s−1 and 14.7° s−1 but not at 27.8° s−1 or higher.
claims.source: We plotted the location of maximal spiking relative to the receptive field centre as a function of velocity for 26 ganglion cells recorded on a multi-electrode array and found that motion anticipation occurred when the bar moved at velocities between 3.8° s−1 (250 μm s−1) and 14.7° s−1 (1000 μm s−1) but not at 27.8° s−1 (2000 μm s−1) or higher (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: Measured experimentally from multi-electrode array recordings.

claims.claim: The computational model closely reproduced the velocity dependence of motion anticipation observed experimentally.
claims.source: This behaviour was closely reproduced by the model (Figure 5A), which also predicted breakdown at velocities higher than ∼14.7° s−1 (1000 μm s−1, Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Computational modeling results matched experimental observations.

claims.claim: Inhibition has a stronger effect over the latter half of the receptive field during motion.
claims.source: But why does inhibition have a stronger effect over the latter half of the receptive field? To investigate the biophysical mechanisms underlying motion anticipation in more detail, we explored a model RGC with a radially symmetric dendritic tree. Figure 6A plots the membrane potential across a dendrite spanning the receptive field as a bar moves across, and compares this to the voltage experienced by the soma. In the absence of inhibition, the somatic voltage was an accurate reflection of the depolarization seen in the dendrites (Figure 6A, left). However, with inhibition present, this was only the case for the first half of the RF, once the stimulus crossed the RF centre dendritic depolarizations had less influence on the somatic voltage.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Inhibitory inputs are most effective at counteracting excitatory inputs when they are located proximally along the dendrite and activated before the distal excitatory synapse.
claims.source: In a landmark theoretical study Koch et al. laid out the conditions that make inhibitory synaptic inputs most effective at counteracting excitatory inputs: (a) inhibitory inputs should be located on the path between the excitatory synapse and the soma (i.e., proximally along the dendrite), and (b) inhibitory inputs should be activated before the distal excitatory synapse (Koch et al., 1983; Liu, 2004; Hao et al., 2009; Pouille et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Cited from theoretical work by Koch et al., 1983 and others.

claims.claim: Excitatory and inhibitory inputs are distributed independently and at uniform density along RGC dendrites.
claims.source: Such an organization might be achieved if developmental processes cause inhibitory synapses to be placed systematically in positions proximal to the nearest excitatory synapse. Such a specific wiring rule does not, however, fit with anatomical studies, which consistently indicate that excitatory and inhibitory inputs are distributed independently and at uniform density along RGC dendrites (Freed and Sterling, 1988; Hitchcock, 1989; Kolb and Nelson, 1993; Owczarzak and Pourcho, 1999; Jakobs et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2008; Schwartz et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Cited from multiple anatomical studies.

claims.claim: Inhibitory synapses outnumber excitatory counterparts in the large majority of RGCs.
claims.source: These two constraints, proximal inhibition across the whole dendritic tree, together with random positioning of synapses, would be satisfied if there are more inhibitory inputs per dendrite than excitatory ones, and this is observed: anatomical studies consistently demonstrate that inhibitory synapses outnumber their excitatory counterparts in the large majority of RGCs (West, 1976; Koontz and Hendrickson, 1987; Freed and Sterling, 1988; Marshak et al., 1988; Hitchcock, 1989; Kolb and Nelson, 1993; Haverkamp et al., 1997; Zhu and Gibbins, 1997; Owczarzak and Pourcho, 1999; Marshak et al., 2002; Jakobs et al., 2008; Koizumi et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Cited from multiple anatomical studies across species.

claims.claim: When the ratio of inhibition to excitation (I/E) was increased, the resultant EPSPs became smaller and the peak of the EPSP shifted forward in time.
claims.source: When the ratio of inhibition to excitation (I/E) was increased, the resultant EPSPs became smaller (Figure 7A) and the peak of the EPSP shifted forward in time (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The generation of motion anticipation requires an excess of inhibitory inputs when synaptic sites are positioned randomly and independently over the dendritic tree.
claims.source: In two of the model ganglion cells, the temporal shift in the time-course of excitation began with I/E > 1, while in the third neuron it began with I/E > 2 (Figure 7C). These observations confirm that the generation of motion anticipation requires an excess of inhibitory inputs when synaptic sites are positioned randomly and independently over the dendritic tree.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The distance between excitatory synapses is surprisingly consistent over the dendritic tree of most ganglion cells and across many species, at ~1 synapse per 5 µm.
claims.source: Several authors have noted that the distance between excitatory synapses is surprisingly consistent over the dendritic tree of most ganglion cells and across many species, at ∼1 synapse per 5 µm (Freed and Sterling, 1988; Jakobs et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2008; Koizumi et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Cited from multiple anatomical studies.

claims.claim: When the synaptic density was reduced to a quarter of its initial value, the critical velocity at which motion anticipation broke down decreased from ≥1 mm s−1 to ~0.5 mm s−1.
claims.source: When the synaptic density was reduced to a quarter of its initial value, while maintaining a constant I/E ratio, the critical velocity at which motion anticipation broke down decreased from ≥1 mm s−1 to ∼0.5 mm s−1 (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: The density of synaptic inputs impinging on a RGC's dendritic tree determines the critical velocity at which motion extrapolation breaks down.
claims.source: It therefore appears that the density of synaptic inputs impinging on a RGC's dendritic tree determines the critical velocity at which motion extrapolation breaks down.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from modeling results showing relationship between synaptic density and critical velocity.

claims.claim: Motion anticipation arises from the passive interactions of excitatory and inhibitory inputs within the dendritic tree.
claims.source: The fundamental observation is that motion anticipation arises from the passive interactions of excitatory and inhibitory inputs within the dendritic tree and three general properties of the retinal connectome: the excess of inhibitory over excitatory inputs in RGC dendrites, the average density of these inputs and their random distribution over the whole dendritic tree.
claims.evidence: Summary conclusion based on experimental and modeling results throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: The amount of motion anticipation is correlated with the RF size in goldfish, with small RF exhibiting the least anticipation.
claims.source: Our measurements in goldfish indicate that the amount of motion anticipation is correlated with the RF size, with small RF exhibiting the least anticipation (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Some parafoveal RGCs in monkey and human have I/E ratios of ~1:1.
claims.source: Indeed, measurements of synapse ratios obtained from electronmicroscopy of parafoveal RGCs in monkey and human indicate that some of these small RGCs have I/E ratios of ∼1:1 (Kolb and Dekorver, 1991; Calkins et al., 1994; Calkins and Sterling, 2007), which would further diminish their ability to perform motion anticipation.
claims.evidence: Cited from anatomical studies in primate retina.

claims.claim: Ganglion cells with the smallest RFs, such as the midget or parvocellular (P) pathway, have the highest spatial resolution but slowest conduction velocities.
claims.source: This observation may make sense in the framework of separate 'what' and 'where' visual pathways (Goodale and Milner, 1992); ganglion cells with the smallest RFs, such as the midget or parvocellular (P) pathway, are involved in coding object detail and correspondingly have the highest spatial resolution but slowest conduction velocities (Gouras, 1969).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous literature on visual pathways.

claims.claim: RGCs with larger RFs, the magnocellular (M) pathway, have high conduction velocities and are involved in coding the spatial location of an object.
claims.source: Whereas RGCs with larger RFs, the magnocellular (M) pathway, have high conduction velocities (Gouras, 1969) and are involved in coding the spatial location of an object relative to the organism, a computation that would obviously benefit from motion anticipation.
claims.evidence: Cited from previous literature and logical inference about functional roles.

claims.claim: The excitatory signal transmitted to RGCs is delayed relative to the retinotopic position of a moving object.
claims.source: We find that the excitatory signal transmitted to RGCs is delayed relative to the retinotopic position of a moving object, indicating that the temporal correction occurs within the ganglion cell (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: Measured experimentally through voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: Motion anticipation is generated by passive interactions within the ganglion cell dendritic tree, and is therefore relatively independent of other computations carried out by the circuitry of the inner retina.
claims.source: Instead, motion anticipation is generated by passive interactions within the ganglion cell dendritic tree, and is therefore relatively independent of other computations carried out by the circuitry of the inner retina.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental and modeling results showing autonomous computation in dendrites.

claims.claim: The non-linear interaction of inhibitory and excitatory synaptic inputs within the dendritic tree shifts the profile of excitation forward in time.
claims.source: It is the non-linear interaction of inhibitory and excitatory synaptic inputs within the dendritic tree that shifts the profile of excitation forward in time.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through modeling and experiments showing how inhibition affects excitation timing.

claims.claim: The classical linear-nonlinear receptive field model incompletely describes the response of a ganglion cell to a moving stimulus.
claims.source: The modelling we carried out as part of this study illustrates why the classical linear-nonlinear receptive field model incompletely describes the response of a ganglion cell to a moving stimulus: excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs interact in a non-linear manner that depends on time and position on the dendritic tree.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from modeling results showing non-linear interactions.

claims.claim: Koch et al., 1983 described the shunting effect of an inhibitory input lying on the path between an excitatory input and the soma as an analogue implementation of a Boolean AND-NOT operation.
claims.source: Koch et al., 1983 have described the shunting effect of an inhibitory input lying on the path between an excitatory input and the soma as an analogue implementation of a Boolean AND-NOT operation in which one input vetoes another.
claims.evidence: Cited from theoretical work by Koch et al., 1983.

claims.claim: The AND-NOT operation is activated when the object moves away from the soma and receptive field centre, aligning the time of peak excitation closer to the time when the object is in the centre of the receptive field.
claims.source: Here we find that this AND-NOT operation is activated when the object moves away from the soma and receptive field centre, aligning the time of peak excitation closer to the time when the object is in the centre of the receptive field.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from modeling results showing how inhibition affects excitation during motion.

claims.claim: Local integration of excitatory and inhibitory inputs in PV-5 cells endows them with sensitivity to approaching objects.
claims.source: For example the local integration of excitatory and inhibitory inputs in PV-5 cells endows them with sensitivity to approaching objects (Münch et al., 2009), whereas in directionally selective ganglion cells dendritic Nav channels are used to boost their direction sensitivity (Schachter et al., 2010; Sivyer and Williams, 2013).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous studies on dendritic computations in specific RGC types.

claims.claim: NMDA receptors selectively boost EPSPs that move centripetally along a dendrite.
claims.source: For example, NMDA receptors selectively boost EPSPs that move centripetally along a dendrite (Branco et al., 2010), such a mechanism could augment motion anticipation in guinea pig OFF α RGCs where NMDA receptors make a significant contribution to visually evoked spiking but not in OFF ∂ or ON α RGCs where NMDA receptors are less conspicuous (Manookin et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous studies on NMDA receptor function in dendrites.

claims.claim: Dendritic spikes combined with gap junction coupling allow a specific subtype of directionally selective ganglion cell to respond much earlier than expected to motion in its preferred direction.
claims.source: Additionally dendritic spikes combined with gap junction coupling allow a specific subtype of directionally selective ganglion cell to respond much earlier than expected to motion in its preferred direction (Trenholm et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Cited from Trenholm et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Motion anticipation in ganglion cells arises when feedforward inhibitory synapses outnumber excitatory inputs.
claims.source: A fundamental finding of our study is that motion anticipation in ganglion cells arises when feedforward inhibitory synapses outnumber excitatory inputs (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through modeling shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The location of an inhibitory synapse on the dendritic tree of a ganglion cell can have a large effect on the output of that ganglion cell.
claims.source: Our model demonstrates (Figure 6B) that the location of an inhibitory synapse on the dendritic tree of a ganglion cell can have a large effect on the output of that ganglion cell.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through modeling shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The operation of direction-selective ganglion cells results from the particular wiring of their starburst amacrine cell inputs.
claims.source: Indeed the operation of direction-selective ganglion cells results from the particular wiring of their starburst amacrine cell inputs (Briggman et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Cited from Briggman et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Non-midget RGCs receive many more inhibitory inputs than excitatory and these are located randomly over the dendritic tree, independently of excitatory inputs.
claims.source: It has long been recognized that non-midget RGCs receive many more inhibitory inputs than excitatory and that these are located randomly over the dendritic tree, and independently of excitatory inputs (Freed and Sterling, 1988; Hitchcock, 1989; Kolb and Nelson, 1993; Weber and Stanford, 1994; Owczarzak and Pourcho, 1999).
claims.evidence: Cited from multiple anatomical studies.

claims.claim: A surplus of inhibitory inputs on each dendrite ensures that stimuli entering a receptive field are transmitted more effectively to the soma than stimuli traversing the latter half.
claims.source: This characteristic wiring can now be understood in the context of the mechanism generating motion anticipation; a surplus of inhibitory inputs on each dendrite ensures that stimuli entering a receptive field are transmitted more effectively to the soma than stimuli traversing the latter half.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from modeling and experimental results.

claims.claim: Variations in the distance between inhibitory and excitatory inputs will vary the object velocity that provides the most effective shunting of excitation to the soma.
claims.source: Our simulations (Figure 7) and the analysis of Koch et al., 1983; demonstrate that variations in the distance between inhibitory and excitatory inputs will vary the object velocity that provides the most effective shunting of excitation to the soma because this shunting depends on the time delay between these conductances.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through modeling and cited from theoretical work.

claims.claim: The general conditions that generate motion anticipation in the retina also exist in downstream areas of the visual pathway, including the superior colliculus or optic tectum, thalamus and area V1 of the visual cortex.
claims.source: It appears that the general conditions that generate motion anticipation in the retina, topographically organized neurons receiving feedforward inhibition, also exist in downstream areas of the visual pathway, including the superior colliculus or optic tectum (Bollmann and Engert, 2009), thalamus (Blitz and Regehr, 2005) and area V1 of the visual cortex (Miller, 2003; Haider et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Cited from studies of other brain regions.

claims.claim: A topographic organization of sensory inputs combined with feedforward inhibition onto dendrites may be a general mechanism for correcting time delays in neural signals relative to events in the external world.
claims.source: A topographic organization of sensory inputs combined with feedforward inhibition onto dendrites may therefore be a general mechanism for correcting time delays in neural signals relative to events in the external world.
claims.evidence: Speculative conclusion based on observations in retina and citations from other brain regions.

results.result: Motion anticipation is a fundamental retinal computation that compensates for the ~70 ms phototransduction delay, allowing accurate localization of moving objects. This phenomenon is observed across the majority of ganglion cell types and multiple species, with peak firing occurring earlier than expected from flashed stimulus responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C8-C12 establish the biological significance and ubiquity of motion anticipation. The ~70 ms delay (C8) is well-documented in prior literature and confirmed experimentally (C14). The phenomenon is demonstrated across multiple cell types (C12, C16) and species, with functional relevance shown in salamander (C11). These foundational claims are well-supported by both citations and experimental data.

results.result: Experimental characterization in goldfish RGCs shows motion anticipation with peak firing occurring 46 ± 13 ms before the stimulus reaches receptive field center, compared to 62 ± 3 ms delay for flashed stimuli. The degree of anticipation correlates with receptive field size (r = -0.593, accounting for 35% of variance).
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C18 present core experimental findings with appropriate sample sizes (n=25), statistical analysis (Pearson correlation), and consistent observations across cell types. The correlation between RF size and anticipation (C17) is statistically significant and mechanistically interpretable. The observation that cells with smallest RFs show least anticipation (C18) is consistent with the proposed mechanism.

results.result: Voltage-clamp recordings reveal that excitatory inputs to RGCs are delayed (peak EPSC occurring 158 ± 34 ms after bar reaches RF center in 7/9 cells), with no significant difference from linear predictions in most cells, ruling out presynaptic mechanisms of motion anticipation.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C22 provide critical negative results that constrain the mechanism. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (C20) appropriately compares measured vs. predicted responses. The exception in orientation-selective cells (C21, n=2) is noted but represents a minority. These findings effectively rule out bipolar cell terminal mechanisms (feedback/lateral inhibition, synaptic depression) as the primary source of motion anticipation.

results.result: Disrupting inhibition in single RGCs by dialyzing with 120 mM Cl⁻ eliminates motion anticipation, shifting peak firing from -18 ± 11 ms to +210 ± 26 ms (p < 0.0002), while leaving flash responses unaffected. This demonstrates that feedforward inhibition is necessary for motion anticipation.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C26 present a critical causal experiment with appropriate controls. The approach (high Cl⁻ dialysis) is validated by prior work (Taylor et al., 2000) and specifically disrupts inhibition in the recorded cell while preserving circuit function. The selective effect on motion (C24) but not flash responses (C25) strongly supports the conclusion (C26). Statistical significance is appropriate (p < 0.0002, n=6).

results.result: Computational modeling with passive dendrites and physiologically realistic parameters (I/E ratio ~2:1, synaptic density ~1 per 5 μm) successfully reproduces motion anticipation, demonstrating that passive dendritic properties are sufficient for this computation.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 show that computational models with experimentally measured parameters (C27: I/E = 2.1 ± 0.23, n=10) reproduce motion anticipation (C28). The robustness analysis (C29) demonstrates the mechanism works across physiologically relevant parameter ranges but breaks down at extreme values (Rm = 50 MΩ), providing boundaries. The modeling is well-constrained by experimental data.

results.result: Blocking active dendritic conductances (NMDA receptors, voltage-gated Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ channels) with MK-801 and QX-314 does not eliminate motion anticipation, with EPSPs peaking 47 ± 29 ms before stimulus reaches RF center (p = 0.0002, n=7), confirming that active conductances are not necessary.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 provide strong experimental evidence that active conductances are dispensable. The pharmacological approach is well-validated, with verification that drugs reached dendrites (10 min dialysis, compared to Alexa 488 diffusion). The timing of anticipation in passive cells (47 ± 29 ms) is statistically indistinguishable from control cells (46 ± 13 ms, p = 0.9844), strongly supporting the conclusion.

results.result: Motion anticipation operates at velocities between 3.8° s⁻¹ and 14.7° s⁻¹ but breaks down at 27.8° s⁻¹ or higher, with computational models accurately reproducing this velocity dependence.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 demonstrate quantitative agreement between experimental data (n=26 cells, multi-electrode array) and model predictions. The velocity range is consistent with prior work in salamander (cited). The model's ability to predict breakdown velocity provides validation and suggests the mechanism captures essential biophysics.

results.result: Inhibition preferentially affects the latter half of the receptive field during motion because proximal inhibition activated before distal excitation effectively shunts excitatory inputs. Anatomical studies show that inhibitory synapses outnumber excitatory inputs and are randomly distributed on RGC dendrites, satisfying the conditions for effective shunting across all motion directions.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 integrate modeling insights (C34) with established theoretical principles (C35, Koch et al., 1983) and extensive anatomical literature (C36-C37, multiple citations across species). The mechanism explains how random synaptic placement with excess inhibition achieves direction-invariant motion anticipation. The logic is sound and well-supported by both modeling and anatomical data.

results.result: Computational modeling demonstrates that motion anticipation requires an excess of inhibitory over excitatory inputs (I/E > 1 in most models, I/E > 2 in one), with increasing I/E ratio causing smaller EPSPs and forward temporal shift in peak response.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 and C57 show systematic modeling results testing the I/E ratio requirement. The finding that I/E > 1 is necessary (C39) is tested across three different RGC morphologies, providing generality. The variation (I/E > 1 vs. > 2) across models suggests some dependence on dendritic architecture, which is appropriately noted. This is a key mechanistic prediction.

results.result: The density of synaptic inputs determines the critical velocity for motion anticipation. Reducing synaptic density to 25% of normal decreases critical velocity from ≥1 mm s⁻¹ to ~0.5 mm s⁻¹. The conserved excitatory synapse spacing of ~1 per 5 μm across species explains the consistent critical velocity observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 and C7 link anatomical observations (C40, multiple citations) to functional predictions through modeling (C41). The relationship between synaptic density and critical velocity is mechanistically interpretable and explains cross-species consistency. The modeling systematically varies density while holding I/E ratio constant, properly isolating the variable of interest.

results.result: Motion anticipation is computed autonomously within each ganglion cell's dendritic tree through passive, non-linear interactions of excitatory and inhibitory inputs, independent of other retinal circuit computations. The excitatory signal transmitted to RGCs is delayed, indicating temporal correction occurs postsynaptically.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C43, C48-C50 present the central mechanistic conclusion, supported by multiple lines of evidence: delayed excitatory inputs (C48, experimental), persistence with passive dendrites (C30-C31), and modeling results (C28, C43). The autonomy claim (C3, C49) is supported by the finding that excitation is delayed while output shows anticipation, requiring dendritic computation. The logic is sound and well-supported.

results.result: Motion anticipation correlates with RF size in goldfish, with smaller RFs showing less anticipation. In primates, parafoveal midget RGCs have I/E ratios ~1:1 and may lack motion anticipation, consistent with their role in the 'what' pathway requiring high spatial resolution, while magnocellular pathway RGCs with larger RFs benefit from motion anticipation for spatial localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 extend findings to functional and evolutionary context. The correlation with RF size (C44) is experimentally demonstrated. The primate data (C45) comes from anatomical studies. The functional interpretation (C46-C47) regarding 'what' vs. 'where' pathways is well-grounded in established visual neuroscience and provides a coherent framework for understanding species/cell-type differences.

results.result: The classical linear-nonlinear receptive field model incompletely describes RGC responses to motion because excitatory and inhibitory inputs interact non-linearly in a spatiotemporally dependent manner. This implements an AND-NOT operation (Koch et al., 1983) that is activated when objects move away from the soma, aligning peak excitation with the object's actual position.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 provide theoretical interpretation of the mechanism. The inadequacy of linear models (C51) is demonstrated by the modeling results showing non-linear interactions. The connection to AND-NOT logic (C52-C53) appropriately cites theoretical work and applies it to explain the directional asymmetry in inhibitory effectiveness. This provides conceptual clarity to the mechanism.

results.result: Other RGC types use dendritic computations for different functions: PV-5 cells integrate inputs locally for approach sensitivity, direction-selective cells use dendritic Nav channels, and some DS-RGCs combine dendritic spikes with gap junctions for enhanced temporal responses. NMDA receptors could potentially augment motion anticipation in specific RGC subtypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 place findings in broader context of dendritic computation. These are appropriately cited from prior literature and serve to illustrate that different RGC types use dendritic mechanisms for various computations. The speculation about NMDA receptors (C55) is appropriately tentative and based on known properties. This contextualizes but does not constitute primary findings.

results.result: The location of inhibitory synapses on dendritic trees significantly affects RGC output, as demonstrated for direction-selective cells with specific starburst wiring. However, motion anticipation relies on general wiring principles: random, independent distribution of excess inhibitory inputs ensures effective transmission of stimuli entering the RF while attenuating later portions, with inter-synapse distance determining velocity tuning.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62 contrast specific vs. general wiring principles. The importance of synapse location (C58) is demonstrated by modeling. The contrast with direction-selective cells (C59) highlights that motion anticipation uses different organizational principles. The interpretation of anatomical data (C60-C61) in light of the mechanism is logical. The velocity tuning prediction (C62) follows from modeling and theory.

results.result: The general conditions for motion anticipation (topographically organized neurons receiving feedforward inhibition) exist in downstream visual areas including superior colliculus, thalamus, and V1, suggesting this may be a general mechanism for correcting neural signal delays relative to external events.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 are speculative extrapolations beyond the retinal data. While the cited studies show feedforward inhibition exists in these areas, they do not demonstrate motion anticipation or test whether the specific mechanism operates there. The speculation is reasonable and appropriately tentative, but lacks direct experimental support. This represents a hypothesis for future work rather than a supported conclusion.
